objectives: Identify the major soil horizons and their agronomic significance.
Explain cation exchange capacity (CEC) and its role in nutrient retention.
Describe how soil pH affects nutrient availability and how liming corrects acidity.

slides.title: Soil profiles, texture, and structure — the physical foundation
slides.body:
Soil is not merely dirt. It is a complex, living mixture of **mineral particles, organic matter, water, air, and billions of living organisms** — the most biodiverse habitat on Earth per unit volume. Understanding soil is the prerequisite for all agronomic management.

**Vasily Vasilyevich Dokuchaev** (1846-1903), a Russian geographer and natural scientist, is recognized as the founder of soil science (pedology). In his 1883 masterwork *Russian Chernozem* (*Russkiy Chernozem*), Dokuchaev was the first scientist to describe soil as a **natural body** formed by the interaction of parent material, climate, topography, organisms, and time — the five soil-forming factors later systematized by **Hans Jenny** in *Factors of Soil Formation* (1941). Dokuchaev also established the concept of the **soil profile** — the vertical cross-section of a soil from surface to bedrock, organized into **horizons**.

**Soil horizons** (from surface down):
- **O horizon** (Organic): surface accumulation of plant litter in various stages of decomposition. Present in forests and undisturbed grasslands; often absent in tilled agricultural soils.
- **A horizon** (Topsoil): the zone of active biological activity, darkened by **soil organic matter (SOM)** and humus. The A horizon is where most crop roots feed and where farmers focus management. Typical depth: 15-30 cm.
- **E horizon** (Eluviation): a leached, pale layer beneath the A where clay and oxides have been washed downward by percolating water. Common in humid, forested soils.
- **B horizon** (Subsoil): the zone of **illuviation** — accumulation of clay, iron oxides, and organic matter leached from above. Roots penetrate the B but encounter harder, less fertile conditions.
- **C horizon**: weathered **parent material** — partially broken-down rock. Little biological activity.
- **R horizon**: unweathered bedrock.

The depth and quality of the A horizon are the primary determinants of a soil's natural fertility. The legendary **Chernozem soils** (Black Earth) of Ukraine and the Great Plains of North America — with A horizons 60-100 cm deep and SOM contents of 5-12% — are among the most productive agricultural soils on the planet.

**Soil texture** refers to the proportions of **sand** (0.05-2.0 mm), **silt** (0.002-0.05 mm), and **clay** (<0.002 mm) particles. These three fractions combine in continuous proportions; the **USDA soil texture triangle** (developed at the USDA Bureau of Soils in the early 20th century) assigns a **texture class** — sandy loam, clay loam, silty clay, loam, etc. — to any combination. Texture is permanent: you cannot change it by management.

**Key textural effects**:
- **Sandy soils**: coarse, well-drained, low water-holding capacity, low CEC, prone to leaching; warm up fast in spring.
- **Clay soils**: fine, poorly drained (high shrink-swell), high water-holding capacity, high CEC, slow to warm; prone to compaction.
- **Loam soils** (~20% clay, ~40% silt, ~40% sand): often considered ideal for crop production — good drainage, moderate water-holding capacity, moderate CEC.

**Soil structure** describes how individual particles **aggregate** into clumps (peds). Good structure — stable **granular aggregates** in the topsoil — creates **macropores** for water infiltration and gas exchange, and **micropores** for water storage. Structure can be improved (cover crops, reduced tillage, organic matter additions) or destroyed (heavy tillage, compaction, raindrop impact on bare soil). The work of **Edward Faulkner** (*Plowman's Folly*, 1943) and the modern **no-till movement** — championed by researchers including **Rattan Lal** (Ohio State University, Borlaug Food and Agriculture Prize 2020) — reflects the understanding that soil structure is a crucial, manageable asset.

slides.title: Cation exchange capacity, soil pH, and liming
slides.body:
Two of the most important chemical properties for soil fertility management are **cation exchange capacity (CEC)** and **soil pH**.

**Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC)** is the total capacity of a soil to hold positively charged ions (**cations**) — primarily calcium ($\text{Ca}^{2+}$), magnesium ($\text{Mg}^{2+}$), potassium ($\text{K}^+$), sodium ($\text{Na}^+$), and hydrogen ($\text{H}^+$) — in an exchangeable, plant-available form on the surfaces of **clay minerals** and **soil organic matter (SOM)**. These surfaces carry a permanent or pH-dependent **negative charge** that electrostatically attracts and holds cations.

CEC is expressed in **milliequivalents per 100 g soil (meq/100g)** or equivalently in **cmol(+)/kg**. Typical values:
- Sandy soils: 1-5 meq/100g (few clay and organic surfaces).
- Loam soils: 10-20 meq/100g.
- Heavy clay soils: 20-50 meq/100g.
- Pure organic matter (humus): 100-200 meq/100g.

The practical importance of CEC: a soil with a high CEC can **store more plant-available nutrients** and is less prone to **nutrient leaching**. Adding organic matter (compost, manure, cover crops) increases CEC and is one of the most effective long-term fertility investments a farmer can make. This principle was quantified in detail by **Selman Waksman** (Rutgers University) in his studies of humus chemistry in the 1920s-1930s; Waksman received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1952 for the discovery of streptomycin, but his soil organic matter research is equally foundational.

**Soil pH** is the negative log of the hydrogen ion concentration in the soil solution: $\text{pH} = -\log_{10}[\text{H}^+]$. The scale runs from 0 (extremely acid) to 14 (extremely basic); pH 7 is neutral. Most agronomic crops grow best in the range **pH 6.0-7.0**, where the availability of macro- and micronutrients is optimized. 

**pH and nutrient availability**: at low pH (<5.5), aluminum ($\text{Al}^{3+}$) and manganese ($\text{Mn}^{2+}$) become soluble and toxic to roots; phosphorus is fixed by iron and aluminum oxides (low availability). At high pH (>7.5), iron (Fe), zinc (Zn), manganese (Mn), and boron (B) become less soluble. Molybdenum (Mo) is the opposite — it becomes more available at high pH.

**Liming** is the application of calcium carbonate ($\text{CaCO}_3$, agricultural limestone) or calcium-magnesium carbonate (dolomitic limestone) to raise soil pH. The neutralization reaction is:

$$\text{CaCO}_3 + 2\text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{Ca}^{2+} + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2$$

The amount of lime needed to raise soil pH depends on the **buffer pH** — the soil's resistance to pH change (its buffering capacity) — which is itself a function of CEC. A sandy, low-CEC soil requires little lime to change pH; a heavy clay or high-organic-matter soil requires much more. Lime recommendations in the US are typically given in **tons per acre (t/a)** of agricultural limestone, calculated from the **SMP buffer test** (developed by **Shoemaker, McLean, and Pratt**, 1961) or similar methods.

**Soil organic matter (SOM)** is the sum of all organic materials in soil — living organisms, fresh residues, partially decomposed material, and stable humus. SOM is central to soil fertility because it: (1) supplies nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur through microbial **mineralization**; (2) increases CEC and water-holding capacity; (3) binds soil aggregates; (4) feeds the soil food web; (5) sequesters carbon. A 1% increase in SOM in the top 20 cm of a hectare of soil represents approximately 26 tonnes of organic matter and roughly 1 tonne of additional plant-available water. The target of achieving **'4 per 1000'** — a 0.4% annual increase in SOM globally to offset CO₂ emissions — was proposed at the COP21 climate conference in Paris (2015), drawing on research by **Dominique Arrouays** and colleagues at INRAE (France).

slides.title: The soil food web and soil testing
slides.body:
Soil is not a passive nutrient reservoir — it is a living ecosystem. The **soil food web** (a concept popularized by **Elaine Ingham** and colleagues at Oregon State University in the 1980s-1990s) describes the complex food chain that begins with plant roots and dead organic matter as energy sources and proceeds through bacteria, fungi, protozoa, nematodes, arthropods, earthworms, and larger organisms.

**Key players**:
- **Bacteria**: the most numerous soil organisms (~100 million per gram of fertile topsoil). **Nitrogen-fixing bacteria** — *Rhizobium*, *Bradyrhizobium*, and free-living *Azospirillum* — convert atmospheric $\text{N}_2$ to ammonium ($\text{NH}_4^+$) in a biologically irreversible step. Boussingault's 1838 observation that legumes enrich soil nitrogen was finally explained biochemically in 1960 when **Howard Gest** and colleagues established the enzymatic mechanism of **nitrogenase** (covered in depth in Lesson 3).
- **Fungi**: form networks (hyphae) that extend the effective root surface area. **Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF)** — forming symbioses with >80% of terrestrial plant species — dramatically extend the volume of soil explored for phosphorus and water. The symbiosis was first systematically described by **Albert Bernhard Frank** (1885), who coined the term 'mycorrhiza.' Applied AMF inoculants are now a commercial product.
- **Earthworms**: *Lumbricus terrestris* and related species are the 'ecosystem engineers' of temperate soils. **Charles Darwin**'s last book, *The Formation of Vegetable Mould, through the Actions of Worms* (1881), quantified their contribution to soil formation — Darwin estimated earthworms pass 25-50 tonnes of soil per hectare per year through their bodies. Modern research confirms their importance in aggregate stability, organic matter turnover, and drainage.
- **Nematodes**: microscopic roundworms, both beneficial (bacterivores, fungivores) and damaging (**plant-parasitic nematodes** such as *Heterodera glycines*, the soybean cyst nematode, cause >$1 billion in US yield losses annually).

**The nitrogen cycle in soil**: organic nitrogen (in plant residues, manure, SOM) is converted to plant-available forms by microbial **mineralization**: organic-N → ammonium ($\text{NH}_4^+$, held on CEC sites) → nitrate ($\text{NO}_3^-$, mobile in soil water, prone to leaching or **denitrification** back to $\text{N}_2$ in anaerobic conditions). Managing this cycle — timing fertilizer applications to match crop demand, using nitrification inhibitors, incorporating legumes into rotations — is a central challenge in sustainable agronomy.

**Soil testing** is the farmer's primary diagnostic tool. A standard agronomic soil test (typically run by a university extension lab or commercial lab) measures: pH, P (often by the **Mehlich-3** or **Bray P1** extractant), K, Ca, Mg, CEC, organic matter (by loss-on-ignition or dichromate oxidation), and sometimes micronutrients (Zn, B, Fe, Mn, Cu). Results are compared to **crop-specific critical levels** developed through field calibration trials — work pioneered in the US by **Roger Bray** (Illinois), **Evan Peck** (Iowa State), and **Emit Kamprath** (North Carolina State) in the 1950s-1970s.

Soil testing reduces both over-application of fertilizers (reducing cost and environmental impact) and under-application (reducing yield loss). The **4R Nutrient Stewardship** framework — **Right Source, Right Rate, Right Time, Right Place** — developed by IPNI (International Plant Nutrition Institute) and endorsed by the FAO, makes soil testing the starting point for every fertilizer recommendation. A soil test is, in Liebig's language, the tool that identifies which stave in the barrel is the shortest.

question.question: Which soil horizon is the primary zone of biological activity, organic matter accumulation, and plant nutrient uptake — and therefore the most critical for agronomic management?
options: The B horizon (subsoil), because it accumulates clay and iron oxides leached from above.
The C horizon, because it contains unweathered parent material with the highest mineral content.

The A horizon (topsoil), darkened by soil organic matter, with the highest biological activity, the greatest root density, and the highest nutrient-supplying capacity. Dokuchaev's 1883 description of the Russian Chernozem — with its deep, humus-rich A horizon — established this as the key indicator of soil productivity. Protecting and building A horizon depth and organic matter content is the foundational goal of sustainable soil management.
The O horizon, because it contains the freshest organic material for immediate nutrient release.
question.explanation: The A horizon is where the action is agronomically. It contains the highest concentrations of soil organic matter (darkening the color), the highest microbial biomass, the densest root populations, and the greatest cation exchange capacity. The O horizon is important in forests but is typically absent or very thin in tilled croplands. The B horizon is relevant for deep-rooting crops but has lower fertility. The C horizon is parent material with minimal biological activity. Vasily Dokuchaev (1846-1903) established the soil profile concept, and the depth and quality of the A horizon is the primary indicator of natural soil fertility — which is why erosion that removes topsoil (A horizon) is so damaging and so difficult to reverse on a human timescale.

hints: Think about where roots and microbes are most active.
Dokuchaev described this as the key horizon in his 1883 Russian Chernozem study.
slides.workedSolution: The A horizon (topsoil) is the primary zone of biological activity and nutrient cycling. Its depth, organic matter content, and CEC are the main determinants of natural soil fertility. Protecting it from erosion and building it through organic matter management are the central goals of soil conservation.

question.question: A soil has a CEC of 15 meq/100g and a base saturation of 70% (meaning 70% of the CEC is occupied by basic cations Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, K⁺, Na⁺). The remaining 30% is occupied by H⁺ and Al³⁺ (acid cations). How many meq of acid cations are held per 100 g of this soil? Give a whole number.
question.hint: Acid cation saturation = 100% - 70% = 30%. Acid cation load = 30% × 15 meq/100g = 0.30 × 15.

question.question: Lime requirement calculation
question.goal: A farmer's soil test shows pH 5.4 and a buffer pH of 6.2 (measured by the SMP buffer method). The lime recommendation table for this state says: for buffer pH 6.2, apply 2.5 t/ha of agricultural limestone (calcium carbonate equivalent, CCE = 90%) to reach pH 6.5. Calculate the actual tonnes per hectare of the commercial lime product the farmer must purchase.

steps.prompt: Step 1: What does CCE = 90% mean, and why must we adjust the recommendation?
steps.motivation: Commercial lime is rarely 100% pure CaCO₃; the CCE correction ensures we apply enough neutralizing equivalents.

acceptedAnswers: CCE 90% means the lime is 90% as effective as pure CaCO3; we need more of it to deliver the same neutralizing effect

hints: If the product is only 90% as reactive as pure lime, you need to apply more tonnes to get the same pH change.
steps.reveal: CCE (calcium carbonate equivalent) expresses liming material quality relative to pure CaCO₃ (CCE = 100%). A CCE of 90% means each tonne of this product neutralizes only as much acidity as 0.90 tonnes of pure CaCO₃. To deliver the same neutralizing power, you need to divide the pure-lime recommendation by the CCE fraction.

steps.prompt: Step 2: Calculate the actual tonnes per hectare of commercial lime needed. Round to 2 decimal places.
steps.reveal: Actual rate = 2.5 t/ha ÷ 0.90 = 2.78 t/ha. The farmer must purchase and apply approximately 2.78 tonnes per hectare of the commercial lime product to achieve the same pH-raising effect as 2.5 t/ha of pure CaCO₃. If the farmer applies only 2.5 t/ha of the 90%-CCE product, soil pH will not reach the target of 6.5 and some nutrient availability problems will persist.

question.prompt: In ≤150 words, explain how soil organic matter improves soil fertility through at least THREE distinct mechanisms, and name two scientists whose work established the importance of SOM. Use the terms CEC, mineralization, and soil structure in your answer.
question.rubric: Answer should cover at least three of: (1) SOM increases CEC (negative charge from humus holds more nutrient cations); (2) microbial mineralization of SOM releases plant-available N, P, and S; (3) SOM binds aggregates, improving soil structure, macroporosity, aeration, and water infiltration; (4) SOM increases water-holding capacity (each gram of humus can hold several grams of water); (5) SOM feeds the soil food web (energy for bacteria, fungi, etc.). Should name at least two scientists: e.g. Selman Waksman (humus chemistry, Nobel 1952), Rattan Lal (SOM and carbon sequestration, Borlaug Prize 2020), Elaine Ingham (soil food web), Charles Darwin (earthworms and organic matter, 1881), or Vasily Dokuchaev (first to describe SOM-rich Chernozem, 1883). Must use CEC, mineralization, and soil structure correctly.
